stops.title: The whole graph
stops.text: 1,729 nodes and 10,069 edges. Top to bottom: why it exists, what the code does, what proves it. Every point is a row the loop wrote.

stops.title: Where it comes from
stops.text: A requirement has to come from somewhere it can be checked against: here, a named source.

stops.title: The requirement
stops.text: A requirement, a node of its own. Everything below hangs off it.

stops.title: The step that needs it
stops.text: A use case step binds it into a chain of cause and effect.

stops.title: Claude's reasoning
stops.text: One step of a written argument. It cites the requirement and the code, and the graph checks those two really are joined.

stops.title: The code
stops.text: A method, a node of its own. The reasoning cites it by name, and a name the code does not have fails the run.

stops.title: One decision
stops.text: A branch of that method, and the requirement that owns it. This link is how code maps to requirements.

stops.title: Broken on purpose
stops.text: One break of that decision. It runs alone against the tests, and one of them has to fail.

stops.title: Caught
stops.text: The test that caught it failed when this break ran. That is the requirement being held.

stops.title: And one that got past
stops.text: No test caught this break. Either it changes nothing, and that has to be proven, or a test is missing.

stops.title: The readers
stops.text: Each large node outside the rings is one thing the harness tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Its rays go to what it reads. Solid has reached its goal, hollow has not, and a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt.

stops.title: Trying is not reaching
stops.text: Goal: who owns new code. It is trying, and it has not got there. The score below is against the plain rule it has to beat.

bp-whole.title: All the floors
bp-whole.tip: Every part of the system, each floor a Blueprint.

bp-agent.title: The agent at work
bp-agent.tip: What an agent does when someone asks it for a change. The tools below hold it to account; this sheet is the part only an agent can do.

bp-pass.title: One pass
bp-pass.tip: One command runs all of it, in this order. The numbers on the nodes come from a real pass on the kit's example, a small wallet and store in C#.

bp-breaking.title: Breaking the code
bp-breaking.tip: A coverage tool says a line ran. This asks whether any test would notice if the line were wrong. It never touches the live project; it works in a sandbox.

bp-requirements.title: The requirements, as data
bp-requirements.tip: The owner's words become a model a machine can check. Nothing here looks at whether the code works yet; this tests the requirements themselves.

bp-graph.title: The record, and 17 questions of it
bp-graph.tip: The graph is what the loop believes. Each criterion is one question asked of it, named for the mistake it would catch. A hole of ours fails the run; a hole of the owner's is a question.

bp-stats.title: The stats choose what's next
bp-stats.tip: Each pass measures itself. A stat nothing reads is a cost with no use, and the audit says so. The same shape sits one level up, where stats are the code, triggers the requirements and ticks the tests.

bp-tick.title: The standing tick
bp-tick.tip: A fresh agent with no memory, one item, the same stat measured before and after. Nothing starts a tick for you; schedule one or don't.

bp-learned.title: What learns, and has to earn it
bp-learned.tip: A graph network that proposes links, a small model that predicts which breaks get past the tests, and a list of goals. Each is measured against a plain rule on data it never saw, and stays off if it loses.

bp-measure.title: Does it help? On against off
bp-measure.tip: The honest measure. Two agents get the same prompt and only one gets the loop. The harness measures what they made, and graders who cannot see which is which judge it.

bp-ship.title: Shipping it
bp-ship.tip: The kit other developers install, and the public pages. A possible leak fails the build rather than warning about it.

bp-agents.title: Many agents at once
bp-agents.tip: The runtime underneath. Agents share a project through files, not a server, and a stuck worker asks instead of guessing. who.py says who is on what, from their own transcripts.

bp-cpp.title: The full C++ pseudocode
bp-cpp.tip: The whole system as pseudocode for a C++ reader, every function tagged with the real one it stands for.

harmony-1.title: 1. Stat Moved

harmony-2.title: 2. Trigger Fired

harmony-3.title: 3. Pick Names Work
harmony-3.tip: Link 3, pick names work: PASS. The pick of the next work names its area because of the stat.

harmony-4.title: 4. Goal Named

harmony-5.title: 5. Work Ran
harmony-5.tip: Link 5, work ran: NOT WIRED. The work the pick named is launched through the tick's launcher, and its end, or its failure, is on file.

harmony-6.title: 6. Stat Moved Back

harmony-7.title: 7. Lists Changed

harmony-8.title: 8. Growth Point

harmony-9.title: 9. Documents Flagged

harmony-10.title: 10. Graph Holds

tree.label: The guided tour
tree.tip: One real thread through the graph, from where a requirement comes from to the test that caught a break of it.

children.label: 1. The whole graph
children.tip: 1,729 nodes and 10,069 edges. Top to bottom: why it exists, what the code does, what proves it. Every point is a row the loop wrote.

children.label: 2. Where it comes from
children.tip: A requirement has to come from somewhere it can be checked against: here, a named source.

children.label: 3. The requirement
children.tip: A requirement, a node of its own. Everything below hangs off it.

children.label: 4. The step that needs it
children.tip: A use case step binds it into a chain of cause and effect.

children.label: 5. Claude's reasoning
children.tip: One step of a written argument. It cites the requirement and the code, and the graph checks those two really are joined.

children.label: 6. The code
children.tip: A method, a node of its own. The reasoning cites it by name, and a name the code does not have fails the run.

children.label: 7. One decision
children.tip: A branch of that method, and the requirement that owns it. This link is how code maps to requirements.

children.label: 8. Broken on purpose
children.tip: One break of that decision. It runs alone against the tests, and one of them has to fail.

children.label: 9. Caught
children.tip: The test that caught it failed when this break ran. That is the requirement being held.

children.label: 10. And one that got past
children.tip: No test caught this break. Either it changes nothing, and that has to be proven, or a test is missing.

children.label: 11. The readers
children.tip: Each large node outside the rings is one thing the harness tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Its rays go to what it reads. Solid has reached its goal, hollow has not, and a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt.

children.label: 12. Trying is not reaching
children.tip: Goal: who owns new code. It is trying, and it has not got there. The score below is against the plain rule it has to beat.

children.label: 13. The whole graph
children.tip: Fly anywhere: drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, W A S D to move. Point at a node to see what kind it is.

tree.label: Blueprint of the whole system
tree.tip: The whole agent harness as a Blueprint you can watch run.

children.label: Watch it run
children.tip: One request through the whole system, replayed from a recording of a real pass.

children.label: All the floors
children.tip: Every part of the system, each floor a Blueprint.

children.label: The agent at work
children.tip: What an agent does when someone asks it for a change. The tools below hold it to account; this sheet is the part only an agent can do.

children.label: One pass
children.tip: One command runs all of it, in this order. The numbers on the nodes come from a real pass on the kit's example, a small wallet and store in C#.

children.label: Breaking the code
children.tip: A coverage tool says a line ran. This asks whether any test would notice if the line were wrong. It never touches the live project; it works in a sandbox.

children.label: The requirements, as data
children.tip: The owner's words become a model a machine can check. Nothing here looks at whether the code works yet; this tests the requirements themselves.

children.label: The record, and 17 questions of it
children.tip: The graph is what the loop believes. Each criterion is one question asked of it, named for the mistake it would catch. A hole of ours fails the run; a hole of the owner's is a question.

children.label: The stats choose what's next
children.tip: Each pass measures itself. A stat nothing reads is a cost with no use, and the audit says so. The same shape sits one level up, where stats are the code, triggers the requirements and ticks the tests.

children.label: The standing tick
children.tip: A fresh agent with no memory, one item, the same stat measured before and after. Nothing starts a tick for you; schedule one or don't.

children.label: What learns, and has to earn it
children.tip: A graph network that proposes links, a small model that predicts which breaks get past the tests, and a list of goals. Each is measured against a plain rule on data it never saw, and stays off if it loses.

children.label: Does it help? On against off
children.tip: The honest measure. Two agents get the same prompt and only one gets the loop. The harness measures what they made, and graders who cannot see which is which judge it.

children.label: Shipping it
children.tip: The kit other developers install, and the public pages. A possible leak fails the build rather than warning about it.

children.label: Many agents at once
children.tip: The runtime underneath. Agents share a project through files, not a server, and a stuck worker asks instead of guessing. who.py says who is on what, from their own transcripts.

children.label: The full C++ pseudocode
children.tip: The whole system as pseudocode for a C++ reader, every function tagged with the real one it stands for.

children.label: 1. Stat Moved
children.tip: Link 1, stat moved: PASS. The worse value is in the log, and the trend reads it as worsening.

children.label: 2. Trigger Fired
children.tip: Link 2, trigger fired: PASS. An improvement requirement on the stat fires.

children.label: 3. Pick Names Work
children.tip: Link 3, pick names work: PASS. The pick of the next work names its area because of the stat.

children.label: 4. Goal Named
children.tip: Link 4, goal named: PASS. The Stats List names the goal that reads the stat, and a requirement that reads it.

children.label: 5. Work Ran
children.tip: Link 5, work ran: NOT WIRED. The work the pick named is launched through the tick's launcher, and its end, or its failure, is on file.

children.label: 6. Stat Moved Back
children.tip: Link 6, stat moved back: PASS. The tick that targeted the stat has a measured outcome: the stat's own value before and after.

children.label: 7. Lists Changed
children.tip: Link 7, lists changed: PASS. The Goals List and the Stats List are rewritten by the tick that finished.

children.label: 8. Growth Point
children.tip: Link 8, growth point: PASS. The growth page is rebuilt by the tick and draws the stat's new readings.

children.label: 9. Documents Flagged
children.tip: Link 9, documents flagged: PASS. The tick says which documents describe the stat, from the graph.

children.label: 10. Graph Holds

slide-cover.head:
Slide 1 of 28: TNT Tools · internal training manual

How to use AI for games

The words on this slide

How to use AI for games

Adapted for Heavy Iron. Requirements first, tested by AI, so nothing is a guess.

99%

accurate: 99.03% of 35,951 blind derivations, from a graph that abstains rather than guesses

7 of 11

task pairs went to the loop, with three blind graders judging each

3 of 3

public targets, a version parser, a JSON object and a game’s scoring rules, each held a fault we could run

The full manual, in plain words: every claim here, and the test behind it

What the speaker says

This is how we use AI at TNT Tools: our internal training manual, adapted for you. Three measured numbers to start. The 99% is from our knowledge graph, on facts: 99.03% of 35,951 derivations it had never seen were right, and when it cannot back an answer it abstains. Seven of eleven pairs went to the loop when three blind graders judged the two answers; slide 23 has the losses and the cost. The third is from three trials on code you can read for yourself: Unreal Engine’s version-string class, its JSON object and the scoring rules of the open-source game osu!. Each held a fault against its own spec or docs, and each was shown by calling the code as shipped; slide 14 has them, and the control run that found careful reading without the loop finds as many. Behind this slide: The real graph of osu!’s scoring rules: 1,062 nodes, drawn from the store the loop wrote.

The slide at full size

90% coverage hid 30 uncaught breaks

The words on this slide

Same code, two measures

90% coverage hid 30 uncaught breaks

A coverage tool said

90%

of lines run, 85% of branches. Unreal’s SemVer parser, with the 2 tests it has.

Break every decision, every way

30

of 236 live breaks got past every test. 14 sat on lines coverage calls covered.

Nothing about the code changed. Only how hard it was tried.

Behind: every break of osu!’s scoring rules. Red: no test caught it.

What was tested, and how

2

What the speaker says

On Unreal Engine 5.7’s SemVer parser, a class that follows the public Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec and has 2 tests, a coverage tool reported 90% of lines and 85% of branches. Breaking every decision every way the tool knows made 246 breaks. 236 were live (the rest did not compile, or were proven by their compiled code to be the same program): 206 were caught and 30 got past every test, and 14 of those 30 sit on lines the coverage tool calls covered. A measure that counts lines run, or breaks code one way, flatters it; that is why the tool breaks every decision every way it knows. The picture is another target, osu!’s scoring rules, where 250 of 536 live breaks got past the three test files that were run. Behind this slide: every break of osu!’s scoring rules and the test that caught it. Red: no test caught it, and each one has to be explained.

The slide at full size

The words on this slide

Measured · every number has its test

What it does on real code

87.3%

of 236 live breaks of Unreal’s SemVer parser caught by a test. 30 got past. JsonObject 69.7%, osu! 53.4%.

48 of 68

statements held by a test: breaking one fails a test. 7 of the 16 requirements taken from the spec have no test about them.

3

requirements the spec leaves unsaid, marked inferred and put to the owner as questions, beside the 16 it states.

13 min

for a full pass over SemVer: 246 breaks, each run alone in a copy, never in the live project. osu!’s 563 took 74: each break of a constructor rebuilds the game.

Half

the work left unfinished: blind graders counted 9 items with the loop, 18 without.

18

ways of being wrong the graph checks, each proven by a planted mistake it must catch.

Where each number comes from

3

What the speaker says

The first four are the three public trials of 30 October, mostly on SemVer: Unreal Engine 5.7’s version-string class, held to the public Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec, with the 2 tests that exist on it. 246 breaks were made and 236 were live; the 87.3% is 206 caught, and 30 got past. The JsonObject and osu! figures are on slide 14, where osu!’s 53.4% is what three test files hold and is low for the game as a whole. A statement is held when breaking it makes some test fail. The 3 inferred requirements are the model’s own: the spec says what is valid, not how a class refuses, and nobody has said which; they go to the owner, never settled by the tool. The pass took 764 seconds on SemVer, about 13 minutes, at low priority on a busy machine. Half the unfinished work comes from 28 blind grades, 6 of them against the hint arm. The 18 are the graph’s criteria: each stops one way of being wrong, and a selftest plants that mistake and must catch it. Behind this slide: osu!’s scoring graph from below: the ring of tests nearest, the requirements furthest.

Slide 4 of 28: The key is accuracy

The gap between a guess and the truth is what people call AI slop

The words on this slide

The key is accuracy

The gap between a guess and the truth is what people call AI slop

Accuracy pays everywhere

It boosts productivity across the board. Our view: in some cases it makes AI thousands of times smarter.

Why the gap opens

Prose can’t be checked. Tests pass for the wrong reason. The context window forgets.

At TNT Tools: no slop

That is the standard. Every value is read from a source, or marked absent with its reason.

616 of 616

top-tier facts right against outside truth

99.2%

right on 209 held-out questions, answering 61% and abstaining on the rest

60M

facts in the graph it reasons over, each carrying its sources

What accuracy has been measured, and on what

4

What the speaker says

The key is accuracy. It boosts productivity across the board, and in our view it makes AI, in some cases, thousands of times smarter; that multiplier is our view, not a measurement, and no multiplier of that size has been measured. The gap between what AI guesses and what is true is what people deem AI slop. These three numbers are from our knowledge-graph work, on facts rather than code, against cached Wikidata as the outside truth, with bars declared before each run. The precision comes from abstaining: asked the same 209 questions, a local language model answered 95% at 98.0%. The numbers on code are on slide 3. Behind this slide: Inside the graph, among the methods.

The words on this slide

Back to 1999!

Requirements first. Long live waterfall.

This is how we review our code: we pour the effort into requirements first. Time to learn systems analysis and design again. Agile is, for the most part, dead.

More requirements, gaps filled, loop closed, nothing is a guess: slopless code.

Hand-crafted quality on an IKEA budget.

What writing them first found in a shipped parser

16

requirements taken from the public SemVer spec, every numbered rule mapped or excluded with a reason

4

faults against that spec, found while writing them, each shown by running the code

7

of the 16 have no test about them, including every rule on which strings are valid

Unreal Engine 5.7’s SemVer parser. Reading the code against each rule found the faults; the breaks found where no test looks.

Behind: the links from requirements down to the code they own.

Requirements first, in plain words

5

What the speaker says

Back to 1999. This is how we review our code: first by pouring our effort into requirements. Time to learn systems analysis and design again. No more agile, it is dead for the most part; long live waterfall. More requirements, gaps filled, loop closed, nothing is a guess, which means slopless code. We want hand-crafted quality on an IKEA budget. The card is the public SemVer trial: the requirements were written from the Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 spec, every numbered rule either mapped to one or excluded with a reason, and writing them against the code found 4 faults that fail when run, such as Compare throwing on the spec’s own example. Be exact about who found what: an agent reading the code against each rule found them, not the breaks, and a control run showed that an agent reading carefully with no tool of ours found the same faults. What the requirements and the breaks add is the count of what no test holds: 7 of the 16 requirements have no test about them. Behind this slide: the links from requirements down to the code they own, in osu!’s scoring rules.

slide-extract.head:
Slide 6 of 28: Requirements make requirements

It extracts new requirements from the ones you have

The words on this slide

Requirements make requirements

It extracts new requirements from the ones you have

Automatic

Each use case step needs something. What no requirement provides becomes a new one, marked inferred, and goes to the owner as a question.

Complete in, accurate out

The more complete the requirements, the more accurate the prompt built from them. Start with the ones that run through the most code.

Epic to code: not measured

The aim is a rough epic grown into a larger set, then code written from it. These trials started from a spec or a game’s own docs. The epic-to-code test has run; its results will be published with the benchmark.

Behind: osu!’s requirements and use cases: one epic, four use cases, 30 requirements. We wrote all 30; the walk inferred none.

How requirements make requirements

6

What the speaker says

The tool’s main intent is to take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case and grow them into a larger set, so that the code written from them is as accurate as it can be. The first card is the mechanism: it walks each use case, and when a step needs a condition that nothing provides, it marks an inferred requirement and sends it to the owner as a question, never as a decision. The second card is our judgment from building with it; no run has measured it directly. The third is the honest state. The trials on public code started from a published spec or from a game’s own doc comments, so their requirements were written from existing words: on osu! all 30 were written and none inferred, and on SemVer 3 of 19 are marked inferred. The end-to-end test, a rough epic grown into requirements and code written from them, graded by tests from an independent source, has run, and its results will be published with the benchmark: the last slide says what it takes. Two earlier tries give no number to lean on: growing a model from three requirements tied with and without the loop, and when two features of ours were joined the walk did not find the places they meet. Behind this slide: osu!’s requirements and use cases.

The slide at full size

slide-firstclass.head:
Slide 7 of 28: What AI is for

There is no such thing as “we don’t use AI”

The words on this slide

What AI is for

There is no such thing as “we don’t use AI”

FIRST

A first-class testing tool

Write every line by hand if you like. It still tells you which of your tests cannot fail, and which code no test notices.

SECOND

A code writer

When it writes code, it is held to the same requirements and the same tests as everyone else.

Keep your tests. There is no reason to throw away really well done tests: that is the baby with the bathwater. They become the judge of what AI does.

Behind: the tests, and every break each one caught.

AI as a tester first, in plain words

7

What the speaker says

The reality is that AI is a first-class testing tool primarily and a code writer second. A team that writes all its code by hand can still point it at its tests: every break it makes must fail a test, and a break that does not is a test you do not have. Nothing here asks you to throw away tests you already trust. They are what it is measured against. Behind this slide: The tests: the green ring, and the breaks each one caught.

The slide at full size

Slide 8 of 28: How it runs

Write the model, then one command

The words on this slide

How it runs

Write the model, then one command

Model

story, requirements, use cases; 19 rules check it

Break

every decision, every way, in one compile

Test

each break alone; a test must fail

Graph

every piece a node; 18 criteria read it

Verdict

HOLDS, or OPEN with its questions

python closed_loop.py run <model> --out REPORT.md

Close what is yours: a missing test, an unclaimed line, a break to explain. The owner’s questions go to the owner. Run again, and lock it once nothing of yours stands.

One pass, end to end

8

What the speaker says

One pass runs from the model to a verdict. Every requirement, use case step, code place, branch, break, test and reasoning step becomes a node in a graph, and each of the 18 criteria stops one way of being wrong, proven by a planted mistake. Holes that are yours you close. Questions only the owner can settle go to the owner. Behind this slide: The graph one pass leaves behind.

slide-breaks.head:
Slide 9 of 28: Breaking the code

Every decision, broken every way

The words on this slide

Breaking the code

Every decision, broken every way

Conditions

negated, made true, made false

Operators

< to <=, equality swapped, && to ||, arithmetic swapped

Values

a number plus one, a bool flipped, a text emptied, an argument defaulted

Structure

ternary arms swapped, an else removed, a statement removed, an early return

When a break survives, there are only two honest answers

It is the same program

Proven by the compiled code: the same IL, set aside. Otherwise it needs a written reason, which lapses when its code changes.

A test is missing

Every claim is pinned to its code’s fingerprint, so a deleted line stales the claim. Our own “same program” claims have been wrong before, and tests now pin them.

Behind: breaks up close. Each point is one way of breaking one decision.

What a break is, and when it is the same program

9

What the speaker says

Up to 24 breaks a statement, one of each kind first. One limit on every: until this week the C# adapter skipped overloads, operators and property bodies without saying so, and it still does not walk a field's value or an indexer, which the report now names; slide 25 has the numbers. A break that survives every test is either a missing test or the same program. Same program is proven by comparing compiled code, Trivial Compiler Equivalence from Papadakis and others, 2015. Anything else needs a reason in writing, and a declared equivalent that a test ever kills is a hole, not a pass. Behind this slide: One stretch of the breaks up close: each point is one way of breaking one decision.

The slide at full size

slide-nodegraph.head:
Slide 10 of 28: The node graph

Everything is one graph, from why to proof

The words on this slide

The node graph

Everything is one graph, from why to proof

How it is laid out

One ring per kind of node, top to bottom: why it exists, what the code does, what proves it. Each branch and each break hangs under its method.

How code maps to requirements

339 links say which requirement owns which decision in the code. 191 say where that decision sits. A decision nobody owns is a hole.

Fly through it: the demo

W A S D, or follow one requirement down to the test that holds it.

1 source

30 requirements, all written

5 use cases, 17 steps

34 methods

200 branch cells

563 breaks, 277 uncaught

168 tests

The graph and the demo, in plain words

10

What the speaker says

This is the actual graph of osu!’s scoring rules, the rules of a shipped rhythm game (ppy/osu, MIT licence), drawn from the store the loop wrote: 1,062 nodes and 5,675 edges, nothing invented and nothing left out. The store itself is SQLite and N-Triples; the rings are how the demo draws it. Each ring is one kind of node. Each branch and each break sits at the angle of the method it belongs to, so a method and everything under it line up. The mapping is two kinds of edge: a branch maps to a requirement, and a branch is at a method. That is how you get from any line of decision in the code to who asked for it, and back. The model has one epic use case, four use cases under it and 30 requirements, all written from the code’s own doc comments; this trial wrote no argument chain, so that ring is empty. The red points are the 277 breaks no test caught: 250 got past every test that was run, 13 are proven by compiled code to be the same program and 14 did not run. The 250 are the work, and they are 250 of the 536 live breaks only for the three test files that were run, not for the game’s whole test project. The fly-through is the same data in three.js: drag to orbit, W A S D to fly, and a tour that follows one real thread. It also has views for just the code-to-requirement links, just the breaks, and just what the graph neural network reads.

The slide at full size

slide-graph.head:
Slide 11 of 28: The record

The graph remembers; closed means no “may” is left

The words on this slide

The record

The graph remembers; closed means no “may” is left

MUST

Authored requirements

The owner wrote them. Each must hold, and a test must notice when it does not.

MAY

Inferred requirements

What the chain needs and nobody wrote. Only the owner settles each one.

Breaking code can refute closure, never prove it: closed is always relative to the breaks tried and the tests that watch.

The graph, and must and may, in plain words

11

What the speaker says

The graph is the record, and the criteria read it. The closest formal idea of closed is the Modal Transition System of Larsen and Thomsen, 1988: every behaviour is marked must or may, and a specification is refined until no may is left. Here the authored requirements are the musts, and the inferred ones the chain needs are the mays. The owner's open questions are exactly those mays. Behind this slide: Inside the graph.

The slide at full size

slide-chain.head:
Slide 12 of 28: Checking Claude’s reasoning

Claude writes its reasoning as a chain; the graph checks every step

The words on this slide

Checking Claude’s reasoning

Claude writes its reasoning as a chain; the graph checks every step

says: "A limited line sells its quantity and is then sold out" cites: [W-3, Store.Buy]

Where it meets the code: the step becomes a node citing two nodes already there. A branch of that method maps to that requirement, so the two join, 2 links apart.

Grounded: a cite that is not there fails the run. Joined: what a step cites must connect within 4 links. Not checked yet: whether the words are true. A real step once said “or” where the code needs both, and it passed.

102

steps in 9 chains, every cite resolved

4

steps that would not join

1 of 1

owner’s question this chain never reached

OWNER: where it is stated

W-3: the requirement

A use case step needs it

Claude’s step cites both

Store.Buy: the code

A branch of it maps to W-3

A break of that branch

The test that caught it

The chain checks, and what they do not check yet

12

What the speaker says

This is how we go after hallucination. When Claude finishes a change it writes down, step by step, why the change does what the requirements ask. A chain is a written argument it produces on purpose, like showing your work; it is not a recording of the model's private thinking. Here is how it meets the code. The chain and every step become nodes in the same graph as the code. Each step has cites edges to the requirement and the method it stands on. A cite to something that is not a node fails the run, so a made-up requirement or a method the code does not have cannot pass. Then the graph walks from one cite to the next: here W-3 and Store.Buy meet because a branch of that method maps to W-3, two links apart. If they do not meet within 4 links, the step is reported; across the on-against-off runs, of 102 steps in 9 chains, 4 would not join, and one agent split its 2 while another reported its 2 as resting on reading alone. An owner's question no step reached is listed as a blind spot; this chain never reached W-4, what a refused purchase does to the stock. The step and the picture are from the kit's example, which you can run yourself: the chain was added to a copy of it and the whole loop run, and it held. Be precise about the limit: it checks what each claim stands on, not whether the claim is true, and no check yet walks on from a step to whether the code it stands on is tested, though the links are there, as the picture shows. It removes the hallucination that invents a source; it cannot promise to remove all of it. And one real step is the proof: a fresh reviewer found it said or where the code needs both. It was grounded and joined, and it was still wrong.

The slide at full size

slide-map.head:
Slide 13 of 28: Early prototype

The requirements map to the code, and the map finds mistakes

The words on this slide

Early prototype

The requirements map to the code, and the map finds mistakes

Every requirement links to the code it owns, in one graph. Its checks and the breaks do most of the finding so far. A GNN learns on the same map, proposes who owns new code, and is set to learn what does not fit.

7 of 16

requirements taken from the SemVer spec that no test is about, every rule on which strings are valid among them

110 of 191

branches of osu!’s scoring rules with a break no test caught, each claimed by the requirement that should have a test

10 of 48

requirements on a public asteroid game resting on behaviour with no value behind it

Next slide: the three public trials side by side, and the bugs.

Behind: only the links from code to requirements.

What the map has found, and on what

13

What the speaker says

It is an early prototype, and it has already found a lot of problems by mapping code to the graph. Be accurate about who found what: so far it is the graph's criteria and the breaks. The graph neural network proposes which requirement owns new code, and using it to flag a claim that does not fit is planned, not measured; slide 16 shows where a plain rule still beats it. The first number is a hole in the map itself: on SemVer, 7 of the 16 requirements taken from the spec have no test about them, found by reading each test against the requirements, before any break ran. The second is osu!’s scoring rules: all 191 branches the tests cover are claimed by a requirement, and 110 of them have a break that got past the three test files that were run, so those are tests missing, not requirements missing. Read it as what those three files hold, and as low for the game as a whole. The asteroid run is public code, language-neutral parts only, with no breaks, because there is no JavaScript adapter yet. The next slide is the three trials on source your team can read, on the same terms. Behind this slide: only the links from code to requirements.

Who found what: an agent reading the code against each rule found the bugs, while writing the requirements. The breaks showed where no test looks. No graph neural network (GNN) played a part. A control run then gave agents the same task without the loop: blind graders found no real fault in only one arm, and the loop cost 1.2 to 1.4 times the tokens.

The numbers, the bugs, and how to re-run it

14

What the speaker says

These are the first numbers a reader can check. Three trials on code outside our own project: two parts of Unreal Engine's own C# and the scoring rules of a shipped open-source game, with requirements from public specs and the code's own doc comments, and no test or product code written. The table's last column is the point for a team that trusts coverage: nearly half of what got past sits on lines a coverage tool calls covered. Read osu!'s 53.4% as what three test files hold, and as low for the game as a whole: its full test project crashed on this machine on the clean copy too. The trials' biggest finding was in our own tool, which silently skipped overloads, operators and property bodies, and failed five other ways on real code. All are fixed with planted tests. Re-run on an earlier target of ours that has no overloads, they changed no verdict and found one real gap, now closed by a test. The budget did not hold either: about 100 minutes and 260,000 tokens against 45 and 150,000 per trial, mostly on those bugs. Behind this slide: osu!'s real graph.

slide-gnnhow.head:
Slide 15 of 28: How it learns

A graph neural network (GNN) proposes what the graph is missing

The words on this slide

How it learns

A graph neural network (GNN) proposes what the graph is missing

How it works

Reads. Each node starts as its own words, hashed to 512 numbers.

Listens. GraphSAGE layers let each node hear its neighbours, relation by relation.

Ranks. A scorer ranks every requirement for a decision with no owner.

Asks. Below 70% sure it abstains. Above, its answer goes out as a question, never a verdict.

Never reads breaks, tests or chains. They hold the answer, and new code has none.

What it records

Score, when a pass runs it: beside the best plain rule, the words alone and random.

Each job, per project and per seed: the next slide. Some verdicts flip with the seed alone.

Breaks ranked: how many survivors the first fifth of a run holds, against the plain rule and random.

What it reads: its nodes and links, and how many of them are owner links.

More requirements: its score by how much of the links it can see.

How sure: at 70% sure, how often it is right, and on how much of the new code.

Every tune: each variant’s score, and what was kept.

How it tries to improve

The stats call it. When its lead over the plain rules falls, the stats name a tune as a next job. It is due after 5 passes anyway.

A tune redraws what it reads: each relation left out, each derived link added.

The bar: kept only if it wins by 0.02, then again on a seed it was not chosen on.

So far: tunes have been run and nothing was kept: no variant won by the bar.

How it works and what it records, in plain words

15

What the speaker says

Be clear what kind of thing it is: a proposer. It proposes which requirement owns new code, and a person or an exact check accepts the proposal; it is never a verdict. Whole methods are held out when it is tested, so the score is on code it has not seen. The picture behind this slide is exactly what it reads, on osu!’s scoring rules: the graph with breaks, tests and chains taken away, because those hold the answer and new code would not have them. Both leaks were measured before they were closed. The stats are all recorded in files beside the model, one row a pass or a tune; a pass adds the score when it is run with the GNN switched on. Scores are mean reciprocal rank, where 1.0 is always ranked first. Once test results exist, a plain rule that reads them beats it, and the next slide shows where. Self-improvement here means this: its lead over the plain rules is a stat. When that lead falls as more tests arrive, the stats report it as worsening and name reshaping the graph as a next job, beside writing tests. It is due after 5 passes without one anyway. A standing tick or a person then runs the tune. So far tunes have been run and nothing has earned a place: no variant beat the full graph by the bar of 0.02. That is the honest state: it attempts to improve itself, and the attempt has not paid yet.

The slide at full size

Each project’s run plan records the verdict: a network is switched on only where it beats the plain rule. Below 70% sure it abstains.

How it was tested, and what the scores mean

16

What the speaker says

The graph neural network, GraphSAGE layers over the graph's typed relations, proposes links: its proposals are questions, never verdicts. Each job is tested on code it never saw, against the best rule that does not learn, and a project's run plan marks it on only if it wins there by more than 0.02. Be accurate about how far that goes: the plan records the verdict, 3 of its 7 lines now reach what a pass runs, wired by the tool's own tick, and all 3 are off today because a plain rule wins. The other 4 are measured only. Every number is a mean over seeds, because a single seed flatters. Some verdicts flip with the seed alone, shown as wins out of seeds. The last two rows have ten seeds, the first two rows five, and the steps row one. The same-program row is doubted: its labels look wrong, and every example it learned from is a break a pass already removes, so the score says nothing about the survivors a person reads. That was found by running the tool on each network, the slides after next. The first three rows are mean reciprocal rank, where 1.0 is always ranked first. The same-program row is the share of proven equivalents in the first fifth of the ranked list. Across projects the learned order did worse than random, so each project trains on its own results. Behind this slide: What the graph neural network reads, from above.

The words on this slide

What they are trained for

The tool’s own code

The score is its own against the plain rule it must beat, by more than 0.02, on code it has not seen, at most seeds.

Next on the list

A second opinion on every claim; what a change will break, before the run; which methods change together; which action moves which stat.

The graph offers more

Links it holds that nothing predicts yet: checked by, asserts, next step, stated by, cites.

The whole Goals List, and how it has changed

17

What the speaker says

Goals are how we understand what we are training for, and trying for one does not mean reaching it. On the tool's own code, 3 of 5 jobs with a result reached their goal, and 1 of those 3 is doubted. A goal is reached only when the learned score beats the plain rule it must beat, by more than 0.02, on code it has not seen, at most seeds. The list is a data file, every number is read from the run that made it, a job no goal claims fails the check, and each run logs what moved, so its history keeps growing. A goal that stops stays on the list, with its reason. A result that reaches the bar is doubted when the same-program goal learned from labels that look wrong on the tool's own code, and every example it learned from is a break a pass already removes. The page says so. We also tried to turn a goal into a vector pointing at what pays off, with its bars and predictions committed in advance; there is a weak direction for what is learnable and none for what saves work, so a person or a tick still chooses, and the page says that too. Behind this slide: only the links from code to requirements.

What it found

A win that is probably not one: it learned a statement’s shape from old labels.

The bar for showing a proposal has no margin, and ignores the rule that wins.

In the first partial run, the code that writes a score was held by no test: 32 of 32 breaks got past.

48 requirements, 144 stats, 32 of them unread. 1,174 of 1,816 breaks caught, 642 got past, none left unrun. Each graph-of-itself score is one seed.

Every network, every flaw, in plain words

19

What the speaker says

The requirements for each learned part are now a subgraph of their own: one use-case model per part, the stats it reads and records as a closed list inside that model, and all of them joined in one graph of 3,298 nodes where 30 stats are shared across parts. The loop then ran on each, breaking its code, and each part was run on a graph of itself. No part beat the plain rules on its own code: four lost and two were too thin to say. That is one seed each, so do not read those scores as means. The best find is the first one on the slide: remove the guard that keeps the answer out of what a network reads, and that network's own selftest still passes. Only a new guard, written from the requirement, catches it; in the first, partial run, 115 of the 369 catches came only from those new guards. The second: one result on the Goals List reaches its bar on labels that look wrong, inferred and not re-run, so it is marked doubted there. None of these flaws is fixed yet; they are on the board. This is not yet the improvement model itself under the rules, which stays an open item, and a longer run has since given every one of its 1,816 breaks a verdict, so the break counts in the table are complete, not lower bounds. Behind this slide: the real graph, from below.

slide-selfimprove.head:
Slide 20 of 28: It tests itself

Self-improvement is on by default

The words on this slide

It tests itself

Self-improvement is on by default

ON

Every pass

Records 44 stats about itself, checks them against the tool’s own rules for improving, and names what to improve next.

Overhead: about a third of a second and 3 printed lines.

OFF

Some tokens saved

Run with --no-self-improve, or set self_improve: false in the model. A pass saves little.

The real spend is the standing tick, which ships in the kit and which you schedule: about 200,000 to 290,000 tokens a tick so far.

NOT NETWORKED HERE

One shared graph

We share ours across the team as a retrieval store (RAG) to save tokens: agents look up what is proven instead of re-reading it.

This version keeps one graph per checkout. Add sharing in whatever way suits your network.

Behind: the tool’s own graph.

Self-improvement, in plain words

20

What the speaker says

Self-improvement is on by default because the tool tests itself. Every pass writes one row of stats, checks them against requirements on those stats, and prints what to improve next. That is cheap. A standing tick costs far more: a fresh agent takes one item, measures before and after, and records whether it was worth it. Tokens here are the app's count for each agent, and nothing starts a tick for you. How far a shared graph cuts tokens has not been measured in this version, which is not networked, and no agent has been timed using a graph in place of the files. Behind this slide: The tool's own graph: its own requirements, its own code, its own breaks.

The slide at full size

slide-selfloop.head:
Slide 22 of 28: The loop, in pseudo C++

One pass, then one tick

The words on this slide

The loop, in pseudo C++

One pass, then one tick

// One pass. Self-improvement is on by default. Verdict run(Model& m, bool selfImprove = true) { Breaks b = Mutate(m.code); // one compile Results r = RunEachAlone(b, m.tests); Graph g = KnowledgeGraph(m, r); Holes h = Criteria(g); // 18 checks if (self_improve_on(m, selfImprove)) { Row row = PassStats(m).collect(); // 44 stats MorphLog(m).add(row); auto fired = improvement::fires(rules, log); Print(NextImprovement(log, fired).picks()); } return h.ours.empty() ? HOLDS : OPEN; }

// One tick. A fresh agent, one item, no memory. void Tick() { Start s = loop_tick::start(); // the lock if (s.stopped || s.busy || s.idle) return; if (s.epochStarts) Brainstorm(); // every 12 RunSelftests(); // red = item telemetry_audit(); // unread = item Item i = Choose(improvement::check(), board); Stat before = i.stat.Measure(); i.Do(); // one change Stat after = i.stat.Measure(); if (s.epochEnds) { run_plan::decide(); // parts on or off improvement::graph(); // did it work? } loop_tick::finish(i, before, after, worth); }

The same shape, one level up: stats are its code, triggers its requirements, ticks its tests. Three ticks worth “no” in a row and it sleeps until something changes.

The recursive graph, in plain words

22

What the speaker says

The toolkit is written in Python; this is pseudo C++ for a C++ audience, and the lower-case names are the real ones in the code: self_improve_on, improvement fires and check, loop_tick start and finish, telemetry_audit, run_plan decide, improvement graph. Left: one pass, which is what an agent runs. If self-improvement is on, it writes a row and prints the stats' picks. Right: one tick, the standing job. A fresh agent, no memory, chooses one item: a red selftest first, then an unread stat, then a fired trigger, then the board. It measures the same stat before and after. Every 12 ticks is an epoch: the first tick brainstorms, the last benchmarks, re-decides which parts run and asks whether the improvements worked. The improvement graph is checked the way the requirement graph is. Behind this slide: Inside the tool's own graph.

Same task, two agents, three blind graders

The words on this slide

On against off · measured

Same task, two agents, three blind graders

5 to 1

for the loop, first round

2 to 2

in the repeat, 1 split

1.2 to 2.3×

the tokens

3 to 55×

What the graders counted

Scope creep: 4 with the loop, 10 without. Invented values: 17 and 5, so it writes more down, and some of that is a guess.

Where it lost, 3 grades to 0

A model-only task, twice: it pinned code on requirements that do not cover it. A repeat: it removed a public constructor and the loop still said HOLDS. And a tie: growing a model from 3 requirements, 16 of 24 each once the code’s requirement ids were removed.

A cheap hint alone

No loop, only a list of weak spots: about half the tokens. Graders chose the loop twice and tied once, for what it wrote down, not for better code.

The tasks, the grades and the harness

23

What the speaker says

Six small tasks, then five of them again: eleven pairs, each with a hidden test neither arm saw. Almost every answer passed its hidden test either way, so correctness is not what separates them on small tasks; what differs is what gets written down and what gets left unfinished. One grader per pair was too noisy: with one grader 3 of the 5 repeats reversed, with three only 1 reversed and 1 split. All three graders agreed on 7 of the 11. The fault counts come from the 28 newer grades, on briefs with the arm's tells removed; 6 of those grades compare the loop to the hint arm. The first grade of each pair is on an older brief, which could name the arm in a few cases. The loop's losses are now planned checks. The tie matters most: the first grow run read 19 of 24 against 10, but the code cited its requirement ids, so both arms started with more than the seed. With the ids removed it was 16 of 24 each, 14 of 46 grown requirements matching a real one with the loop and 12 of 41 without, at 1.6 times the tokens and 4.6 times the minutes, one run each, and neither arm asked for anything it should not see. So recovering a model is not where the loop has shown a gain. Behind this slide: osu!’s scoring graph from above.

Slide 24 of 28: Among the other tools

31 tools, one rubric: 1st or 10th, by the weights

The words on this slide

Among the other tools

31 tools, one rubric: 1st or 10th, by the weights

All 17 criteria count once

A tool's score is the share of the most it could get.

The 9 a team names first

Chosen before any tool was scored: ask, gather, start, install, editor, existing code, team, adoption, price.

Why the place moves

7 of the 17 checks are the ones the loop was built for, and most tools score 0 on them: counted alone we reach 95.2 . On the 9 a team names first we reach 48.1 . Over 10,000 random weightings we are in the top third in 99.9% . The answer is a range, not a place.

Where we lead, where we trail

Lead: breaking the code and requiring the owning requirement's test to notice; no ranked tool scores 3 there. Trail: adoption ( 0 stars), and asking a person good questions from nothing, since we ask only from holes in a chain that already exists. First use, editors and team review: 1 of 3 each.

How far to trust it

We scored ourselves, by the same anchors. One point off every score of ours puts us 8th at equal weights. Docs only, nothing installed; 'absent' means not found on the pages read, and a vendor's own claim is capped at 1 of 3.

The method, and every tool with its page

24

What the speaker says

The owner asked for every agent requirements tool we could find, ranked, and ourselves ranked by the same rubric. The rubric was committed before any tool was scored, with 17 criteria: ten that other tools are good at and we may not be (asking a person good questions, gathering from documents, first use, install, editors, existing code, team review, adoption, price, licence) and seven the loop was built for (finding holes, tying requirements to code and to tests, proving a test catches a break, checking the agent's argument, keeping requirements true, measured evidence). Each score is read from the tool's own page and carries a link; a score with no page behind it is refused by a check with planted failures. 31 other tools were read, 28 of them ranked beside us, 15 with released code. On equal weights we are 1st at 70.6. On the 9 criteria a team names first, a choice made before scoring, we are 10th at 48.1, behind OpenSpec. On the seven deep criteria alone we are 1st at 95.2. We predicted we would not be first on equal weights and would be in the lower half on the team list; both predictions were wrong, and the place still moves by 9 places with the weights, so we say it depends on them. The scores are ours: one point off each takes us to 8th at equal weights. Other tools beat us on 8 of the criteria; the plan has eight items to take those abilities, ranked by what each would move, with the licence of each idea named.Behind this slide: the manual's section on the other tools lists every one with its page.

Each limit, and each target, in plain words

25

What the speaker says

Used where it does not fit, it can be worse than not using it at all. The prototype card is the first trial on code your team can read: the C# adapter skipped overloaded methods, operators and property bodies without saying so, so on Unreal's SemVer.cs it saw 35 of 68 statements and on JsonObject.cs 213 of 288. An earlier target of ours has no overloads, which is why its numbers never showed it. All of that is fixed with planted tests, re-running that target changed no verdict, and the report now names what it still does not walk: a field's value and an indexer. How thin is too thin is not known yet. The two targets are for agents writing code with the loop, shown dashed because neither has been measured there; the 99% on the cover is on facts, from the knowledge graph. The on-against-off harness exists to measure both targets, and the token figure is always being re-evaluated. slide-edge.head:
Slide 26 of 28: What you are getting

Look closely at the secret sauce

The words on this slide

What you are getting

Look closely at the secret sauce

Where it comes from

A mutation of our ARC3 self-improvement loop: a piece of a failed attempt at AGI, which is why it distrusts its own numbers. Ours is internal, so this version was made for you.

How new it is

An independent search found about 8 of its 10 parts are known work. The whole, used as an agent’s done gate, looks new, at medium confidence.

A small edge, for now

As harnesses improve, this will become common knowledge. Today it sets you apart from companies using code generation like a chatbot.

Where it comes from, and what it measured there

26

What the speaker says

This is the method we use ourselves, the secret sauce of TNT Tools. The harness is a piece of a failed attempt at AGI. That attempt's autonomous self-improvement run went 16 days and found nothing that generalized: a counter that could be gamed rose while the honest number stayed flat. That failure is why every stat here must have a reader, a control and a fresh reviewer. Its best agent, a weak proposer with a strong verifier, reached 31 of 63 games where random reached 14. As harnesses improve this will become more common knowledge, so the edge is small and it is for now. Our graph is shared across the team as a retrieval store; this version is not networked, and you could add that in whatever way suits your network. slide-next.head:
Slide 28 of 28: What is next

From a rough epic to code that is right

The words on this slide

What is next

From a rough epic to code that is right

What the tool is for

Take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case, grow them into a larger set, and write the code from that set as accurately as we can measure.

The question

If the requirements for something very difficult are complete and checked, how far does that move what an AI can build?

Measured so far

How much of existing code its tests hold: 87.3%, 69.7% and 53.4% of breaks caught on three public targets. In a control run on two of them, an agent reading carefully found as many faults as the loop did.

NOT MEASURED

The epic-to-code test has run. Its results will be published with the benchmark.

The direction is better tools for making video games. It is not a claim about general intelligence.

What is measured, and what is not

28

What the speaker says

The tool’s main intent is to take the requirements for a game from a rough epic use case and grow them into a larger set, so that the code written from them is as accurate as it can be. The question on the right is a question and not a result: if we have the requirements to do something very difficult, how does that change the landscape for the AI? What is measured is narrower. On three public targets, a version parser, a JSON object and a game’s scoring rules, it measures how much of existing code its tests hold, and that held up against careful reading: a control run gave agents the same task with and without the loop, and blind graders found no real fault in only one arm. What is not shown here is the thing the intent names. The epic-to-code test has run, and its results will be published with the benchmark. The trials on these pages started from a published spec or a game’s own doc comments, and a first try at growing a model from three requirements tied with and without the loop. The test starts from one rough epic for a small game whose right answers come from an independent published source. Agents write the code with and without the grown requirements, and hidden tests written from that source, never from our model, grade both blind. Tokens per arm are recorded, and so are how many requirements the epic grew into and how many the hidden tests needed that it missed. The direction is more advanced tools for making video games, and not general intelligence.

goals.head:
The goals

The readers

Each large node outside the rings is one thing the loop tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Trying is not reaching: solid has reached its goal, a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt, hollow has not got there, and a faint ring is only planned.

  • Who owns new code: Has not reached it.
  • Which tests catch a break: Reached on 1 of 2.
  • Which steps carry a requirement: Has not reached it.
  • Which breaks change nothing: Reached, but doubted.
  • Which breaks will get past the tests: Reached its goal.
  • Where to add a test: Uses another goal's model.
  • A second opinion on every claim: Planned.
  • What a change will break, before the run: Planned.
  • Which methods change together: Planned.
  • Which action moves which stat: Planned, waits for 20 measured outcomes.

So far

  • Graph network reached its goal on 1 of 6 results; small model on the break's features reached its goal on 4 of 4 results (2 of them doubted) (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • 3 of 10 results change with the random seed alone, so no single run settles one (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • Giving a goal more of the graph to read helped by more than the bar in 0 of 6 tries (an anecdote: 6 results).
  • Goals where each answer belongs to about one source, in a sparse table, beat a plain rule far more often than the rest. That says where plain rules are weak, not where work is saved (right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs, and 6 of 7 on goals sealed before they ran (an anecdote at that size)).
  • No rule was found that picks the goals which save work. All 60 of the best candidates were chance or anecdote (52 goals with a measured saving, across 5 domains).
  • Ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can. A learned order beat it on only 2 of 10 goals (10 goals, 31% against 33% saved).
  • The graph offers these next, relations nothing predicts yet: checked by (110 links), asserts (30 links), next step (26 links), stated by (24 links), cites (21 links).

concept-goals.head:
The goals

The readers

Each large node outside the rings is one thing the loop tries to learn: 10 goals, 5 of them trained. Trying is not reaching: solid has reached its goal, a core in a shell is part way there or in doubt, hollow has not got there, and a faint ring is only planned.

  • Who owns new code: Has not reached it.
  • Which tests catch a break: Reached on 1 of 2.
  • Which steps carry a requirement: Has not reached it.
  • Which breaks change nothing: Reached, but doubted.
  • Which breaks will get past the tests: Reached its goal.
  • Where to add a test: Uses another goal's model.
  • A second opinion on every claim: Planned.
  • What a change will break, before the run: Planned.
  • Which methods change together: Planned.
  • Which action moves which stat: Planned, waits for 20 measured outcomes.

So far

  • Graph network reached its goal on 1 of 6 results; small model on the break's features reached its goal on 4 of 4 results (2 of them doubted) (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • 3 of 10 results change with the random seed alone, so no single run settles one (a pattern to test: 10 results from 2 projects).
  • Giving a goal more of the graph to read helped by more than the bar in 0 of 6 tries (an anecdote: 6 results).
  • Goals where each answer belongs to about one source, in a sparse table, beat a plain rule far more often than the rest. That says where plain rules are weak, not where work is saved (right 80% of the time against a 48% base, on 44 goals across 5 graphs, and 6 of 7 on goals sealed before they ran (an anecdote at that size)).
  • No rule was found that picks the goals which save work. All 60 of the best candidates were chance or anecdote (52 goals with a measured saving, across 5 domains).
  • Ordering tests by a plain rule already saves most of what ordering them can. A learned order beat it on only 2 of 10 goals (10 goals, 31% against 33% saved).
  • The graph offers these next, relations nothing predicts yet: checked by (110 links), asserts (30 links), next step (26 links), stated by (24 links), cites (21 links).

help.head:
Help

How to use this page

Pick anything in the tree on the left and the camera flies there, with its page open down here. Pick it again, or use the bar at the top of this page, and the page closes. Flying freely leaves the page as it is.

Flying

  • Drag to orbit. Scroll or pinch to zoom. W, A, S, D fly, Q and E go down and up.
  • N and P move to the next and previous item in this part of the tree.
  • Point at a node to see what kind it is. Click or tap it to open its page: the data behind it, then what that kind of thing is. Click a slide or a reader in the world to go to it.
  • The question mark key opens this page.

The tree

  • Up and down arrows move, right opens, left closes, Enter flies. Home and End go to the ends, and typing a letter jumps to it.
  • The filter box finds anything by its words.

The levels and the chain

  • The levels are four graphs you can fly between: the tool pointed at a game, at its own code, at its learned parts and at its own improvement. A world too big to draw whole is thinned, and the line under the title says how many nodes of how many are drawn.
  • Harmony is a path of ten stops, one per link of the chain from a worsening stat to the documents that describe it. Each stop says PASS, FAIL or NOT WIRED from the last recorded run.

Links

  • Every item has its own address, so a slide or a goal can be sent as a link. Copy link is on the bar of this page.
  • A link in a page to something in the tree flies there. A link to the full manual, a concept page or the deck opens a new tab.

On a touch screen

The text of a tooltip is here, and on the page of the item you pick. A long press on a control shows it too.

  • Contents: Shows or hides the tree of everything you can fly to.
  • ‹: The tour's previous stop.
  • Tour: Start or stop the guided tour along one real thread through the graph.
  • ›: The tour's next stop.
  • Whole graph: Fly back to see the whole graph. The page stays as it is.
  • ?: Help: how to fly, and where the manual is.
  • Hide: Hide the tree, for more room.
  • Page: Shows or hides the page for the selected item. Up and down arrows change its height.
  • Previous: The previous item in this part of the tree.
  • Next: The next item in this part of the tree.
  • Copy link: Copy a link that opens on this item.

Where the rest is

  • The whole manual, as one document.
  • The deck, as slides.
  • The first page.

world-games.head:
Level 1 of 4

Requirements about a game

The tool's requirements for a small game feature, the code that meets them, every break tried on that code and the tests that caught it. It is the graph the rest of this page first showed.

What is drawn

Drawing all 1,729 nodes and all 10,069 lines.

  • 27 requirements, 54 methods, 45 tests
  • 1,104 breaks tried on the code: 974 caught by a test, 55 got past every test, and 75 have no verdict (they did not build, or no test covers their file). The last two are the red nodes.

What the level above is checking

The level above is the tool's own code (the next world up). Its requirements say what the tool must do to a graph like this one: find every decision, break it every way it knows, and say which tests caught each break. The same method breaks the tool's own code: 1,639 breaks were tried, 989 were caught, 648 got past every test and 2 have no verdict.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. Its passes write the stats, and the goals learn from this graph.

world-tool.head:
Level 2 of 4

Requirements about the tool itself

The same kind of graph, drawn for the tool's own code: its requirements, its methods, every break tried on them and the tests that caught each one.

What is drawn

Drawing 1,800 of 2,365 nodes and 3,852 of 6,272 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.

  • 20 requirements, 38 methods, 131 tests
  • 1,639 breaks tried on the code: 989 caught by a test, 648 got past every test, and 2 have no verdict (they did not build, or no test covers their file). The last two are the red nodes.

What the level above is checking

The level above is the six learned parts. They are networks trained on graphs like this one, to guess which requirement owns new code, which breaks change nothing and where to add a test. They are held to requirements by the same method, so their code has a graph too: 1,816 breaks were tried on it, 1,174 were caught, 642 got past every test and 0 have no verdict.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. The stats are written by passes on every level, this one included.

world-learned.head:
Level 3 of 4

Requirements about the learned parts

The same kind of graph for the six small networks that learn from the other graphs, with the jobs they do and the stats they read joined in.

What is drawn

Drawing 1,800 of 3,298 nodes and 3,218 of 8,863 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.

  • 48 requirements, 67 methods, 90 tests
  • 1,816 breaks tried on the code: 1,174 caught by a test, 642 got past every test, and 0 have no verdict (they did not build, or no test covers their file). The last two are the red nodes.
  • 6 jobs a network does
  • 144 stats they read

What the level above is checking

The level above is the improvement model. It reads the stats that every level writes, this one included, and asks of each: is it read, and does it trigger something? It holds 33 requirements, 4 of whose triggers have fired and 3 of those have no answer from a tick yet.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. This world is what the goals about the learned parts are measured on.

world-improve.head:
Level 4 of 4

Requirements about improving the loop

The registry of what each stat must trigger: a requirement per stat, the action it asks for, and the ticks that answered. It is a graph built from the registry and the tick ledger.

What is drawn

Drawing all 90 nodes and all 70 lines.

  • 33 requirements, one per stat, each saying what a pattern in the stat must trigger
  • 4 triggers fired on the last passes, 3 with no answer yet
  • 5 ticks on the ledger, 0 with a measured outcome
  • its own health, read on 2026-10-30 09:24: 2 banked records, learnable not yet

What the level above is checking

There is no fourth world. The improvement model writes its own health back as stats (stats that are read, triggers that are answered, ticks that named their stat), and the same registry watches them, so the tower closes on itself. The rules that check the other three levels have not been run on this one: it is drawn from the registry and the tick ledger, and not from a model they have walked.

Readers

The goals and the stats are the loop reading itself. They stand round the first world, and both are one click from here: the goals and the stats. The stats are written by passes on every level, this one included.

worlds.head:
The recursion

The tool, pointed at itself, three times

The tool holds code to written requirements by breaking the code on purpose. Pointed at a game, that is level 1. Pointed at its own code it is level 2, at the networks it contains level 3, and at the way it improves itself level 4. Each is a real graph read from the store the tool wrote, standing in space where you can fly to it.

  • Level 1: Requirements about a game. Drawing all 1,729 nodes and all 10,069 lines.
  • Level 2: Requirements about the tool itself. Drawing 1,800 of 2,365 nodes and 3,852 of 6,272 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.
  • Level 3: Requirements about the learned parts. Drawing 1,800 of 3,298 nodes and 3,218 of 8,863 lines. The rest are thinned breaks and decisions; every red break is drawn.
  • Level 4: Requirements about improving the loop. Drawing all 90 nodes and all 70 lines.

Across the four worlds 5,419 of 7,482 nodes are drawn. A world too big to draw whole is thinned, every break no test caught is kept, and each page says how many of how many.

A world with no graph still stands here and says why it is empty. None is empty today: all four have a graph.

harmony.head:
Harmony

Do the stats, the learned parts and the graphs work together?

One stat is made worse on a scratch copy of the tools, and the change is followed through ten links. 9 of 10 hold. 1 is not wired: link 5, work ran. None fails.

  • 1. Stat Moved PASS The worse value is in the log, and the trend reads it as worsening.
  • 2. Trigger Fired PASS An improvement requirement on the stat fires.
  • 3. Pick Names Work PASS The pick of the next work names its area because of the stat.
  • 4. Goal Named PASS The Stats List names the goal that reads the stat, and a requirement that reads it.
  • 5. Work Ran NOT WIRED The work the pick named is launched through the tick's launcher, and its end, or its failure, is on file.
  • 6. Stat Moved Back PASS The tick that targeted the stat has a measured outcome: the stat's own value before and after.
  • 7. Lists Changed PASS The Goals List and the Stats List are rewritten by the tick that finished.
