benchmark.head:
The benchmark

Every test run on the loop

55 tests are on record: 35 passed, 12 failed, 8 unclear and 0 not finished. The bar was written down first for 25 of them. A failed test stays on the record, first.

Some results are not published yet. More is on the way, and this page will grow when they are.
benchmark.foot: The benchmark page

benchmark-failed.head:
The benchmark

What failed, what is unclear, what is not known

Failed (12)

  • How full must the graph be before the network beats the plain rules?: On three of four graphs the network did not stay ahead of the best plain rule. On one graph it did, from half full.
  • Do fresh reviewers find holes the loop passes?: The first review ranked 9 holes and the second 10. The criteria were not complete, and the reviews are why they are more now.
  • Every break of the learned parts, with a verdict: Only 2 of the 6 learned parts reach 80 percent caught, and 642 breaks got past every test.
  • Do the plan's switches hold at more seeds?: Seed 0 was the best of ten on the first project, so the public 64 percent was the top of a range. The honest figure was 50 percent. On the second project, seed 0 alone put the switch off.
  • Does each learned part beat plain rules on the loop's own code?: None of the six beat a plain rule on its own code. Four lost and two were too thin to say.
  • Can a goal be turned into a vector that points at goals worth training?: A weak direction for learnable, none for useful. It failed its bars and no page was made from it.
  • A full pass on the game feature the loop was first built on: 974 of 1,104 breaks caught, 55 survived and 77 holes of the loop's own stand, so the pass exits 1.
  • A pass on the loop's own code: 989 of 1,637 breaks caught, 648 survived, 387 holes of the loop's own stand.
  • Does the loop recover a lost model better, with the ids removed?: With the ids removed both arms recovered 16 of 24. The 19 against 10 claim was withdrawn from the deck and manual.
  • Does the loop find more defects than careful reading?: No grader found a real fault in only one arm. The loop added no defect and cost more.
  • Joining two finished features, does the graph name the seams?: The graph named at best 2 of 23 real seams, and none of the 8 open or in conflict. A word search found 10, an agent reading both models 20.
  • Does the front door's queue reach more of a producer's rules than a plain list of clarifying questions?: The record works (refusals, answers, resume, no repeats) and the first five minutes take two minutes of an agent's work after a one-minute quick install. The questions do not beat asking: the first run of the tool touched none of the 12 rules, and after fixes made on seeing that, the queue still reached fewer than the plain list on both games. About half of its questions are worth asking.

Unclear (8)

  • Twelve agent runs, six tasks, with the loop and without it: All twelve arms passed their hidden tests, so the test did not separate the arms. The blind grading leaned to the loop, with one grader per pair, which proved too noisy.
  • Does it matter which requirements are written first?: On the one graph with many requirements, the three requirements that span the most methods gave the network what a random seed needs all 27 for. On the loop's own model no order beat the plain rule. One seed.
  • Can an agent finish a real task with the kit?: It finished and passed its hidden test, but the paired run without the loop also passed, at less cost, and the blind grader preferred the arm without it. One pair.
  • Are the documents tool's own checks held by breaks?: The first pass let 46 of 281 breaks through; after new tests the second pass caught all but one, and one more removal has not been through a further pass.
  • Three blind graders per pair instead of one: Seven pairs favoured the loop, three the other arm and one split. Three graders agreed on only 7 of 11 pairs, and the tasks are small.
  • Does every tool have a selftest, and does it pass?: Every selftest that ran passed in the last measurement, 60 of 60, taken by benchmark.py --survey-selftests on 2026-10-31 on a copy of the tools (72 tools in all); the measurement before it was 60 of 60, and the one before that 57 of 57, taken by prove_all.py with the selftests running several at once. In the measurement before, autobot/dictation_proof.py had exited 1 while X5 was still being built. A passing selftest says little about how much it checks, and 12 tools have none.
  • Did each standing tick find something worth its minutes?: All five ticks said yes about themselves. That is five opinions of the party that did the work.
  • A real argument chain on the kit's example: One step, one run, and no bar fixed first. It shows the checks run end to end on a real step and that the loop still holds; it does not show they catch a wrong one.

Not known

  • Whether a person outside the project can install and run it from nothing, and how long that takes.
  • How many documents describe a requirement in words the rules cannot see.
  • Whether the public numbers stay true when a record changes.
  • Which parts of the loop earn their keep.
  • How much better the loop is than not using it, for each stat.
  • What kill rate a plain mutation tool gets on the same tests.
  • How many real faults a class holds, so faults found per token can be bounded.
  • Whether the learned parts do better on other kinds of code.
  • Whether the loop helps an agent that writes code, as opposed to one that audits.
  • The manual's two stated targets: 95 percent accuracy or better, and up to 90 percent fewer tokens.
  • An outside judgement of whether the standing ticks were worth their minutes.
  • Whether any stat other than the owner network's score is followed through every link of the loop.
  • Tests run before 26 October on the earlier tools of the project.
benchmark-failed.foot: The benchmark page

benchmark-tests.head:
The benchmark

Every test

55 tests, failures first on the benchmark page. Open one for its question, its bar and how it can fail.

Are the links from documents to requirements correct? Passed

The question. When the loop says a manual section, slide or README paragraph describes a requirement, is that so? A wrong link is one whose document does not describe the node it is tied to.

The bar. At least 19 of 20 links correct on each of 3 fresh seeds, read against the source line.

How it can fail. Fewer than 19 of 20 correct on any seed. The first reading, before the seeds, found 2 wrong and 1 worthless of 36; each was fixed as a class with a plant before the seeds were drawn.

Does every link by name stand on the line it cites? Passed

The question. For every link made by a name found in a document, does the file and line it cites really contain that name?

The bar. 0 mismatches on every graph.

How it can fail. Any link whose cited line does not hold the name.

Does attaching documents change anything else? Passed

The question. Adding documents to the graph must not move any other criterion, count or exit code. Did it?

The bar. On the game feature and the kit's own model, no criterion's line other than the new one changes between the old code and the new, and the exit code does not change.

How it can fail. Any line other than the new criterion's differs between old tools and new, or an exit code differs. Each guard that keeps documents out of fingerprints, distance and the network's view was removed in memory and the figure moved.

Does the documents tool refuse what it should? Passed

The question. Does the tool refuse a fabricated requirement id, a renamed section, a missing file, an empty document set and an unparseable document, each in its own test?

The bar. The plan item asked for a plant for each guard. No number was set first.

How it can fail. A planted fabricated id, renamed section, lost document, empty set or unparseable file must each be refused with a named reason.

Are the documents tool's own checks held by breaks? Unclear

The question. The loop breaks code and asks whether a test notices. Break the documents tool's checks the same way: do its own tests notice?

The bar. None set before the passes. The plan asked only whether the plants are themselves held.

How it can fail. A break of the tool's own checks that no test catches.

Do the growth charts refuse a bad log and draw only what the logs hold? Passed

The question. Does the growth page draw every point from a dated log row, break a line where what was counted changed, and stop on a missing or unreadable log rather than guess?

The bar. The plan item named a plant for each rule. No number was fixed first.

How it can fail. Each rule was broken inside a copy of the tool and the selftest had to go red on the check that guards it: lines for any readings, unreadable rows skipped, a join across a change, a missing log, absent read as zero, the gate not called.

Ranking the other requirements tools by a rubric fixed first Passed

The question. Can a ranking of agent requirements tools, our own kit included, be made so that every score has a page behind it and the rubric cannot be bent to flatter the kit?

The bar. The rubric, with 17 criteria, 3 weight profiles and predictions, committed before any tool was scored. Two amendments were committed before a single score.

How it can fail. The tool refuses a score with no evidence, and each refusal is planted in its selftest and seen to fire. A prediction the rubric made can be wrong. Two of six were.

Does the front door's queue reach more of a producer's rules than a plain list of clarifying questions? Failed

The question. From a rough epic, the tool's agent drafts a model and the tool asks the producer the holes of its chain, one at a time. On two invented games whose whole rule sheet the producer holds, does the queue touch more of the rules the epic left out than an agent told to ask clarifying questions, with no kit?

The bar. Committed before any agent saw the epic: the tool earns its place on a game only if its questions touch at least 2 more of the producer's rules than the plain list AND its share of questions touching no rule is within 10 points of the plain list's. Predicted not met. Nine predictions in all, eight held, which is bad news for the tool.

How it can fail. The queue touches fewer of the producer's rules than the plain list, or is noisier. It did on both games: 8 of 12 against 10, and 5 of 10 against 10, by the committed grader. A requirement with no citation, a cite of a sentence that is not there, a quote the sentence lacks, an empty text, an answer that contradicts an earlier one, a question asked twice, a stopped session that repeats a question, an internal id in a question: each is planted in grow.py's or ask.py's selftest and seen to fire beside a control. Each guard broken one at a time in a copy of the tools (break_check.py): the selftest must go red on every break. One run per arm, two invented games, a scripted producer, a blunt grader, my own by-hand reading not blind. A tie within that noise cannot be told from a loss.

Does the skill reach five other agents in the file each reads, from one source, with a stale or invalid copy refused? Passed

The question. The skill is a Claude Code skill. Can its front door, run and prove be written in the layout of Codex and OpenCode, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot and Windsurf from skill/SKILL.md alone, each valid by that tool's own documentation and in the place it names, and can an install write one of them into a project without touching anything else?

The bar. Committed in proofs/L3_prep.md before any layout existed. Five distinct files; each valid by its tool's documented format, under 6,000 characters and under the limits the pages state; each naming the front door, grow, ask, run and prove and how to get the command; all cut from SKILL.md and carrying its hash. A planted missing command, missing file, stale hash, bad front matter and hand edit are each refused, a changed SKILL.md changes all five files when the build runs again, and install --agent writes exactly one file, keeps a user's own text and refuses a file that is not ours.

How it can fail. A layout drops one of grow, ask, run or prove, or a layout file is missing. Each planted and refused. A layout is cut from an older SKILL.md, or edited by hand with its stamp kept. Both planted: the kit check and install --agent refuse. Front matter the tool does not document: a Cursor field it has no name for, globs set on an Apply Intelligently rule, front matter that is not YAML, a Windsurf trigger outside the four, front matter on a plain-Markdown file. Each planted and refused. install --agent overwrites a user's AGENTS.md, a Cursor file that is not ours, or writes outside the project. Planted by giving it a user's own AGENTS.md with CRLF endings and a foreign Cursor file, and by comparing the home folder before and after. An agent does not follow the file, or reads a path the documentation no longer names (Windsurf's page already calls the folder shipped here legacy). Nothing here runs an agent, so this cannot fail in the test.

Does the kit run from one command with no clone, from a package, on a clean home folder? Passed

The question. Can a stranger with Python and no clone run the shipped example through the whole loop with one uvx or pipx command, install the skill, and write another agent's file, with HOME, TEMP and the package cache all empty?

The bar. Committed in this proof before any package existed. uvx --from the built wheel closed-loop-kit try exits 0 and prints HOLDS from a cold cache with every home and temp folder inside a scratch folder; the same from the built source folder and from pipx run if pipx can be had; install --quick ends proved; the wheel holds the tools, the skill, the examples and the layouts; the privacy gate ran on exactly what the wheel was built from; nothing is published.

How it can fail. The wheel lacks a file the tools find by location. Planted by building a wheel without the Python example: try exits 1 and does not print HOLDS. The route a user will take, uvx from the git address, builds from what the repository holds. It has not been run, because the repository does not carry the files until the main session pushes. The built source folder and the sdist stand in for it. A machine with a warm package cache, a clone nearby or another Python would pass what a stranger fails. Each stranger gets a fresh uv cache and an empty working folder; a Python 3.10 interpreter was run once. A slow disk, no network and other systems were not.

Drafting a model from a PRD, a ticket export, a transcript and a public proposal, every requirement citing its sentence Passed

The question. Can a program number the sentences of a PRD, a ticket export, a transcript and a public requirements document, and refuse a draft that does not ground each requirement in a sentence or in a reason, while a second reader reports every rule sentence nothing cites?

The bar. The plan item's done-when, committed in 88eb6aef: one fixture of each kind plus one public document, each requirement citing the sentence and line it stands on, the source_rules check reporting every rule sentence nothing cites, a requirement citing a sentence that is not there refused, counts on file.

How it can fail. A requirement citing a sentence that is not in the text is refused (D2), one citing none is refused (D1), one quoting words the sentence lacks is refused (D4); each is planted and fires. A rule sentence nothing cites is reported by the sentence space (U7) and by source_rules by line; planted. Real markdown broke the first reading (283 half-line sentences on a 400-line proposal, then 3 false uncited hits); both fixed with a case each. Another real document may break it a third way.

How full must the graph be before the network beats the plain rules? Failed

The question. Giving the network 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the links, at what fullness does it first beat every plain rule that does not learn, at every seed?

The bar. The crossover, defined in the tool before the run, is the least fullness from which the network beats every plain rule at every seed.

How it can fail. No fullness from which the network beats the best plain rule at every seed.

Do the plan's switches hold at more seeds? Failed

The question. The run plan switches parts on or off by one seed's score. Would other seeds flip any switch, and was the number quoted in the deck the typical one?

The bar. A guess written on the board before the run - 1 to 3 seeds, 0 or 1 switch flipping - with the flip defined as a gap against the 0.02 margin.

How it can fail. A switch flips at another seed, or the quoted number was the best of the range.

Can a goal be turned into a vector that points at goals worth training? Failed

The question. Leave one domain out. Does a direction learned from the others point at goals that the network can learn, and at goals that are useful, on a graph it has never seen?

The bar. Written before any result and committed with the tool, then the predictions sealed in a second commit before any was trained.

How it can fail. The pooled rank correlation fails the bar on a held-out domain. The plant selftest on invented graphs: a copy of a relation must be refused by the useful direction.

Does each learned part beat plain rules on the loop's own code? Failed

The question. Each learned part of the loop was made a project of its own and the loop was run on it. Did any learned part beat the best plain rule on its own code?

The bar. Whether the network beats the best plain rule that does not learn, the criterion the network is judged by.

How it can fail. The network does not beat the best plain rule, or the graph is too thin to say. Planted known-bad inputs for the new guards must be caught.

Can an agent finish a real task with the kit? Unclear

The question. With the loop switched on and told to use it, can an agent finish a small precisely specified task and pass a hidden acceptance test?

The bar. A budget of 45 minutes and 400,000 tokens was written first; the pass condition was the hidden test.

How it can fail. The hidden acceptance test fails, or the safety flag stops the run. The first three attempts were stopped by the flag.

Twelve agent runs, six tasks, with the loop and without it Unclear

The question. On six small tasks spread over kinds of problem, each with a hidden acceptance test, does an agent with the loop finish better than the same agent without it?

The bar. A hidden acceptance test per task, proven to pass a reference solution and fail the unchanged code before any arm ran, and graders who do not know which arm is which.

How it can fail. A hidden test that passes the unchanged code, or that fails a reference solution, was dropped or fixed before arms ran. Arms read the other arm's notes. A scan found 3 of 27 arms read their run's own events file; the diff now hides what names an arm.

Three blind graders per pair instead of one Unclear

The question. One grader per pair gave a noisy verdict. Does the preference for the loop survive three graders who do not know which arm is which?

The bar. Not set first. The change to three graders was made after the noise was seen.

How it can fail. The three graders split, or most of them prefer the arm without the loop.

Does the loop recover a lost model better, with the ids removed? Failed

The question. A first run said the loop recovered 19 of 24 requirements from code and the arm without it 10. The code cited requirement ids, so the seed was larger than intended. Repeated on code that cites none, does the gap hold?

The bar. The design was fixed first on the board - repeat on code that cites no ids - and the claim stands only if the loop recovers more.

How it can fail. The loop recovers no more than the arm without it.

A small tested class, against a public specification Passed

The question. On a version-number class from a game engine's tools, with only two tests, written against a public specification anyone can read, what do the tests leave open?

The bar. A budget of 45 minutes and 150K tokens, written first. No pass bar for the rate.

How it can fail. The run stops on code it cannot read or compile. It did, six times across the three trials (BP-4 to BP-8 and BP-10), and each cause was fixed with a plant.

A large, well-tested class Passed

The question. On a JSON class with 43 tests, does the loop add anything over a class that is already well tested?

The bar. A budget of 45 minutes and 150K tokens, written first. No pass bar for the rate.

How it can fail. Breaks that no test catches that coverage already marks covered. Many did.

The scoring rules of a shipped open-source game Passed

The question. On a public game's scoring rules (MIT licence), which anyone can open, what do its scoring tests leave open?

The bar. A budget of 60 minutes and 200K tokens, written first. No pass bar for the rate.

How it can fail. A rate read on three test files only, which understates a suite of many more.

Does the loop find more defects than careful reading? Failed

The question. On two of the classes, one agent used the loop and one did not. Three graders who did not know which was which read both reports against what a harness compiled and ran. Did the loop find defects reading did not?

The bar. Not fixed first. The control run was asked for after the first trials, and the question was whether the loop added anything.

How it can fail. No grader finds a real fault in only one arm. That is what happened.

Joining two finished features, does the graph name the seams? Failed

The question. Two finished features of one game were written as models and joined. Does the graph name the places where one needs what only the other provides?

The bar. The list of real seams was written and hashed before any code was opened, and the scoring rule was fixed with it.

How it can fail. The graph names fewer of the real seams than a plain word search. A planted provider must change the causal count: it moved it from 7 to 6, so the zeros are not a dead instrument.

Can the language-neutral parts model public code? Passed

The question. Without any adapter, can the loop read a public game's use-case document into a model and say what is open?

The bar. A budget of 45 minutes and 150K tokens, written first. No pass bar.

How it can fail. A document row the parser cannot read stops the model. The check caught one missing a column.

Does the example run on a machine with only a newer .NET? Passed

The question. Does the kit's C# example run on a machine that has .NET 9 or 10 but not the version it targets?

The bar. A budget of 10 minutes and 20K tokens, written first.

How it can fail. Asked for a .NET version the machine lacks, the run stopped with 'You must install'. That shows the check can fail.

Can a fresh agent install the kit from the zip alone? Passed

The question. A fresh agent with only the zip: does it get the kit installed and running, and what trips it?

The bar. A budget of 30 minutes and 250K tokens, written first.

How it can fail. The agent cannot install, or stops on something the instructions do not say.

Does every recorded stat have a reader? Passed

The question. The loop records many stats about itself. The audit says some are read by nothing. Is the audit itself counting honestly?

The bar. None fixed first. The idea was on the board; the measure was the audit's own count.

How it can fail. Fifteen removals of a piece of the fix each must make a selftest fail. All did.

Does a trigger that fires on every pass say anything? Passed

The question. Improvement triggers fire when a stat changes. Some fired on every pass whatever happened. Do they carry information?

The bar. None fixed first. Found while doing a different item.

How it can fail. Thirteen removals of a piece of the fix must each fail a selftest, on a copy with a passing control.

Do the plan's switches reach a pass at all? Passed

The question. The run plan switches seven parts on or off. Does any switch actually change what a pass runs?

The bar. The check was written first so the reading before and after is one command.

How it can fail. Fourteen removals of a piece of the fix must each fail a selftest. The first run caught 13: an exit-code check was too loose and was tightened.

Did each standing tick find something worth its minutes? Unclear

The question. A recurring tick picks one improvement and does it. Was each tick worth the minutes it used?

The bar. None. The tick judges its own worth.

How it can fail. A tick answering no. None has.

A full pass on the game feature the loop was first built on Failed

The question. Of the breaks made in this feature's code that a test could judge, what share did a test catch, and are there holes of the loop's own?

The bar. Exit 0 means no hole of the loop's own stands. No kill-rate bar is written before a pass.

How it can fail. A break no test catches, or a hole of the loop's own, makes the pass exit 1.

A pass on the loop's own code Failed

The question. Run on its own tools, how much of its own code do its tests hold?

The bar. Exit 0 means no hole of the loop's own stands. No kill-rate bar is written before a pass.

How it can fail. A break no test catches, or a hole of the loop's own, makes the pass exit 1.

The kit's C# example Passed

The question. On the small example shipped with the kit, does the loop reach a clean pass a stranger can reproduce?

The bar. Exit 0 means no hole of the loop's own stands.

How it can fail. A break no test catches on the example. Three survived and are declared to change nothing.

The kit's Python example Passed

The question. The same, for a stranger without a .NET toolchain.

The bar. Exit 0 means no hole of the loop's own stands.

How it can fail. A break no test catches on the example. Three survived and are declared to change nothing.

A real argument chain on the kit's example Unclear

The question. Does one step of Claude's reasoning, citing a requirement and a method of the kit's example, ground and join in the graph the loop writes, with the whole loop still holding?

The bar. The checks as the manual states them before this run: every cite must exist, and every pair a step cites must join within four links.

How it can fail. A cite that is not in the graph fails the run with exit 1. The manual records three planted cases run on a copy of the example: a requirement that does not exist, a method the code does not have, and a step citing nothing. A pair of cites the graph cannot join within four links is reported. None was exercised here.

The last slide says what the tool is for, and what is not measured Passed

The question. Does the deck's last slide state the tool's main intent as a sentence, the hard-requirements question as a question, and plainly what is measured and what is not, with no claim about intelligence?

The bar. The plan item's done_when, written before the slide: the intent, the question as a question, more advanced tools for making video games as the direction and not general intelligence, and what is measured and what is not made plain.

How it can fail. A claim on the slide with no record behind it, or a number the proof cannot trace to a file, fails it. The proof traces each sentence. The public build refuses a name it must not carry. It was run on this slide and found none.

Does every tool have a selftest, and does it pass? Unclear

The question. Each tool should be able to test itself with --selftest. Which tools have one, which pass, and which have none?

The bar. None fixed first. A class count taken now.

How it can fail. A tool whose selftest exits non-zero, rejects the flag, or has none is listed by name. A tool on disk that mentions a selftest and is not in the survey makes the check refuse.

This benchmark's own check Passed

The question. Does the benchmark refuse a proof with no entry, a command naming a missing file, a result that disagrees with its record, and a test with no way to fail?

The bar. The plan item's done-when, committed before the work.

How it can fail. Each refusal is planted in a fixture and must fire, beside a clean control that must pass.

Every break of the learned parts, with a verdict Failed

The question. Of the breaks the loop made in the learned parts' own code, what share does a test catch, now that every break has a verdict and the earlier counts are no longer lower bounds?

The bar. The plan item's done-when, committed first: every break has a verdict. The loop's own standing line for a project is 80 percent caught.

How it can fail. A job below the 80 percent line. Four of the six are. Any break with no verdict. None remain.

Does it matter which requirements are written first? Unclear

The question. Giving the network a fraction of the requirements, does the order they are chosen in change how soon it beats the best plain rule, in random order, most-methods-spanned first, or most-branches-owned first?

The bar. None. The question was asked on the board; no bar was fixed before the run.

How it can fail. No order lets the network beat the best plain rule at any fraction. That is what happened on the loop's own model. A plant shows the pillar order is not just the order of the ids.

Do fresh reviewers find holes the loop passes? Failed

The question. A fresh agent that has not seen the work reads the loop's code and its criteria and ranks the ways a criterion passes while the requirement is not closed. How many did two of them find?

The bar. None fixed first. The loop's own criteria claimed to be complete.

How it can fail. A reviewer finds a hole the loop's checks pass. Both did. Each hole names a plant that reproduces it, and the board marks one fixed only with its plant.

Does the dictation panel turn speech into text and a reply beside the slide on both pages, and keep the key in the tab? Passed

The question. With a key typed into the panel, does pressing Mic turn speech into text, send it to Claude and show the reply beside the slide, on the public deck and on the fly-through, through pauses and from any slide; does every failure say so in words with no substitute reply; and does the key stay in the tab?

The bar. The plan item's done-when and six predictions, written into the proof tool's docstring and committed before its first run; the take's bar and three more predictions written into the same docstring on 10-31 before those checks first ran: every check passes on both pages, no check waived; the dummy key is found nowhere it must not be, and found in each place it is planted; each named failure is said in words.

How it can fail. Planted leaks (the dummy key put in storage, the address, the page title, the console, a file, the address of a call) and the old code of each defect restored in memory (the Mic off at the first pause, no quiet timer, the button in the header, the slide not held, the box cleared on a reply, Close leaving the Mic on, the old resize) must each be caught, and a clean copy must stay quiet. The gate's selftest puts 16 unsafe things into a script or a page (a write to storage, a console line, a second address, a script with a source, a wider policy, a second copy, a key-shaped string) and each must be refused. A script with a source, a replaced fetch, a script added after a key is held, a page over plain http, silence, a browser with no speech, every word the recogniser can end on, a real network failure and ten API failures each make the panel say so in words and ask Claude nothing. The first 135 checks passed while five real bugs stood, because every test spoke six words, was answered at once and started at the top of the page. A use no test walks can still fail.

Do the real API and the real speech service let the dictation panel through, with no key at all? Passed

The question. A browser's route to the API is decided before any key is looked at. With no key anywhere, does the real API's preflight accept the panel's exact headers from the public site's origin, is its refusal readable from a browser, is the panel's version the newest published and each of its models named, and does the panel's own request get out of the page past its policy tag?

The bar. Written into the tool's docstring before its first run: every check passes on both pages, a check that cannot run is a failure, and three controls that must be refused are refused: no opt-in header at the API, no opt-in header in the browser, a host the policy does not name.

How it can fail. The same preflight and request without the opt-in header, and the same request to a host the policy does not name, must each be refused. All were. The same tool on the published page before the fix failed on the script not being the current one, on the Mic stopping at the first pause and on the no-key wording.

Is a change in one stat followed through the triggers, the pick, the lists, the growth page, the documents and the graph? Passed

The question. The stats log, the improvement triggers, the pick of next work, the Goals List and Stats List, the growth charts, the documents and the graphs of the tool were separate tools that each passed their own selftest. When one stat worsens, does the change reach each of the others? One worsening of the owner network's score is planted on a scratch copy of the tool tree and followed through ten links.

The bar. Written in the tool's docstring before the first run. Every link gives a verdict and the evidence it read; a link nothing calls says NOT WIRED and what is missing, never a pass from a stand-in; the real tree is untouched; one chain run takes under 3 minutes and a copy under 150 MB. The docstring predicted 3 of 10 links would hold before wiring.

How it can fail. A link reads FAIL or NOT WIRED. The first run found 6 NOT WIRED and 1 FAIL; wiring moved all but link 5, which stays NOT WIRED with its cost on file. A link passes without a cause: the control run, with nothing worsened, must not report PASS on links 1, 2, 3 or 6.

Does each link's check turn red when only that link is broken? Passed

The question. A chain that has only ever passed proves nothing. For each wired link, one change to the scratch copy breaks only that link (a registry line, a store's edges, a one-line edit of one tool's copy, the old defect put back). Does that link stop reporting PASS, and does any other link go red that does not read what the broken one writes?

The bar. Written in the tool's docstring before the first run. Every wired link has a plant that turns it off PASS, and no link outside its declared dependence turns red. The control (nothing worsened) reports PASS on none of links 1, 2, 3 and 6.

How it can fail. A plant leaves its link at PASS; the run says so ('the plant moved nothing') and exits 1. A plant turns red a link outside its declared dependence. The first matrix run found one: with nothing worsened, link 8 went red because it looked for the worsened value; it now looks for the values the run planted.

Does a finished tick rewrite the two lists, and does the next tick read what they ask? Passed

The question. The Goals List and Stats List logged what moved only when someone ran the writer by hand. Does `loop_tick finish` now rewrite them, rebuild the growth page and name the documents of its stat, say so when a step is skipped, fail loudly when a step fails, and does `start` print what the lists ask? Does a pillar read the lists' check every cycle?

The bar. The item's done_when in the plan: gnn_goals --write in the tick's finish, --check in the pillars, a tick reads what the lists ask. No number was committed before the work.

How it can fail. A finish step is called and does nothing: the tool's selftest runs stub tools and counts which ran and which failed. The finish steps are removed one at a time from the copy and the matching harmony link goes off PASS (links 7, 8 and 9).

Is every number on a public page tied to a record that can say it moved? Passed

The question. Each number on the deck, the manual and the README is a claim. Does a registry place every one of them (read from a record, written by a tool, a name and not a figure, or absent with its reason), re-read the records, and refuse a build when a number no longer matches its record, a record is gone, a new number is unregistered, or a claim reads unpublished work?

The bar. None fixed first. The refusals are the test: each planted and seen to fire, and the gate green on the whole corpus after the registry holds it.

How it can fail. A record that moved, a record that is gone, a reworded sentence, a new unregistered figure, a claim on unpublished work, a malformed claim, a tool's page that would be written differently: each must refuse. A control with none of them must not. A copy of a trial's stats file changed (206 caught to 200): the public build refuses, names the slide and writes nothing. The same copy deleted: it refuses on 47 numbers. A figure claimed by its value and the words of its block can attach to another fact with the same figure and words. The check proves the digits equal the record, not that the sentence means what the record means.

Does every stat that matters have a no-tool value, today's value and a ceiling, each read from a record? Passed

The question. For each stat that matters, can a map say what a capable person or agent gets with no loop, what the loop gives today and the most it could ever give, each figure read from a record or marked absent with its reason and what would bound it? Does it refuse a ceiling below today, a value with no record and a held source on a public section? And what does it say about where the loop has beaten not using it?

The bar. Written into the tool's docstring before the map was assembled: every stat resolves with no refusal and no figure typed in except a ceiling with its arithmetic beside it; the three refusals asked for fire on plants and not on the control; the public section holds no held stat. Prediction, written the same time: on the stats with a like-for-like no-tool value the loop beats it on none of the agent trials, because it cost more on every trial on record.

How it can fail. A ceiling below today, a value with no record, a held source on a public section, a held flag flipped after loading, a proxy read as a beat, a paired count called a beat without a sign test, an absent ceiling read as zero room: each is planted and must be refused or read correctly, beside a clean control. Each rule of the tool broken inside a copy of it, one at a time: the selftest must go red on each. 30 of 30 went red after four plants were added for the four the runs first missed. A ceiling from arithmetic is only as good as the arithmetic: 1.0 for a share cannot be passed and may never be reachable, and a count's floor of zero says nothing about how near it can get. The map marks 1.0 and zero as arithmetic and argues no tighter bound. The agent trials are single runs on one model, so a tie is called within a declared tolerance that was not measured.

Does a stranger get a working, proved install from the README alone, and what does the first run cost? Passed

The question. On a clean home folder, following only the README, does the public kit install, prove itself on its own examples and run the front door with every step giving what the README says and no file of this repository opened; and what does a first run cost in minutes, disk, steps and tokens?

The bar. Committed in the tool's docstring before any fixed run, the baseline having been measured first. Every README step gives its promised exit and text for the four strangers (quick and full, a machine with PyTorch and .NET and one with Python only). No Python process of the run opens a file under the repository, another run folder or the real home. The full install on the machine with PyTorch and .NET takes at most 60 percent of the baseline's time and the quick install at most 120 percent. Every thing that tripped a new user is written down with whether it was fixed.

How it can fail. A README step gives another exit or text. It did: the shipped kit's full install ended INSTALLED WITH FAILURES for all three clean full installs, on a selftest that fails on every Windows home folder. The clean folder lets the real home help the stranger (a warm package cache, a PATH holding dotnet, a temp folder elsewhere): the tool's selftest asks a child where the home, the temp folder and the package cache are, and checks the minimal stranger's python and PATH. A kit that reads the repository would pass on a machine that has it: the audit logs such an open, and refuses itself if a file opened on purpose is not logged. One run per scenario and label on a machine other work was using, at a load that changed between runs and was not recorded for the baseline. A gain the size of the load's swings cannot be told apart from the rows.

Does every proof on record still pass when run again, together, and does the runner refuse the ways to pass without proving? Passed

The question. Run again on a copy of the tools, several at once, every command the record lists and every tool's selftest: how many pass, fail, give no answer, or are not run and why? Does the runner refuse a proof that hangs, one that exits 0 having checked nothing, and one that exits 0 while its own lines or the numbers its entry states say otherwise?

The bar. Committed in the tool's docstring before the first full run. Nothing is dropped, and every item not run carries its reason. The three false passes each have a verdict of their own, planted beside a control. The fast tier finishes in under 5 minutes. A full run takes less than its longest single item plus 3 minutes. Afterwards the record's own check refuses nothing. The real tree is left alone.

How it can fail. A proof that hangs is waited on, or read as a pass. The plant is a program that sleeps for two minutes: it is killed at its limit and named, and the run takes seconds. A tool that exits 0 having checked nothing passes. Planted, and found for real in two tools' selftests, one of which printed no check in the form the others use. An entry whose command exits 0 but leaves a number different from the one the entry states passes. Planted in a fixture record with a command that rewrites the file. The run changes the real tree. The first full run did: a tool's selftest ran git commands that reached the real repository through variables the copy had handed it, and rewrote its index and one setting. Mended; the plant runs git add and commit in the copy and finds the original unchanged. Each guard of the runner broken one at a time in a copy; the selftest must go red on each. 22 of 22 did, after two plants were added for the two that got through. A copy of the tools is not the tree: a command that reads outside the copy fails there, naming the file. 8 of the 14 first findings were that, and each is now added to the copy by name or skipped with a reason.

Does the fly-through show the stats, the learned parts and the graphs working together from real records, and refuse to say a link holds from a stale one? Passed

The question. The fly-through is the manual: a scene with a tree on the left and a page at the bottom. Does it now hold four worlds read from the stores the tool wrote (a game, the tool's own code, the learned parts, the improvement model), each saying how many nodes are drawn of how many; the chain's ten links as a path of stops, each saying PASS, FAIL or NOT WIRED from a record of a real run; and growth, the plan, the benchmark and the proof as pages? And does it refuse a link's state from a record made on tools that have since changed, a held entry reaching a page, and an empty world drawn as nothing?

The bar. fly_manual tree gains plan, growth, proof and harmony; the recursion levels are visible as worlds you can fly between; each with its page.

How it can fail. A link's state is read from a record made on tools that have since changed. Planted: a tool edited after the record, and one deleted; each is refused, and the control passes. A record that does not hold links 1 to 10 once each, names a state the page does not know, has a link with no evidence, or quotes a path on this machine is refused the same way. A held entry reaches a page: its id, its title, its tool or a file only it reads. Planted with a fixture record that holds one entry; the public form passes and the leaked form is refused, and the plan, the proof and the benchmark group each leave a held item out. A world with nothing in it is drawn as nothing. Planted: a store with no node, a store not on disk, an improvement model with nothing in it. Each keeps its tree row, its page, its numbers and a mark, and says why it is empty. A big world is thinned and a red break is dropped, or the numbers on screen do not add up. Planted: every red break and all structure stay, the limit holds, the same store thins the same way, and a break with a verdict the page does not know stops the build. Each guard the page gained made to do nothing, one at a time, in a copy: the selftest must go red. 29 of 29 did. The first run let 3 through (the proof's held-item filter, a relation the page was not told of, a world with no node dropped from the order); each got a plant, one needing its fixture made stricter, and the second run caught all 29. The chain is changed and its record is not run again, so the page cannot be built: that is the refusal working, and it costs about 14 minutes to clear (harmony.py --prove --record).

Does every new group, world and link work for a visitor in a real browser, with WebGPU and with WebGL 2, on a desktop, on a phone and with no graphics? Passed

The question. A browser is driven the way a visitor would: each new tree group is clicked and opens its page, each world flies the camera and says how many nodes are drawn of how many, the goals and the stats are one click from each world and back, each of the ten stops is clicked and must say PASS, FAIL or NOT WIRED as the record does, the page loads no script from anywhere, and the same is done at phone width and with no graphics. Does everything the page promises happen, in both ways of drawing?

The bar. fly_manual tree gains plan, growth, proof and harmony; the recursion levels are visible as worlds you can fly between; each with its page.

How it can fail. A new group or world does not open its page, or does not move the camera, or does not say how many nodes are drawn of how many. Each is a check of the visitor. A link page says a state other than the record's. Each of the ten stops is compared with the record file. Running and looking found nine faults in the first runs, before they shipped: the first world's layer labels drawn over another world, the same sentence twice under a title, an overview of the four worlds that was a white blob with a label out of frame, two links standing on one node, a world's label cut at the edge of a phone, a count that included the chain's ten stops, a pinch on a phone that zoomed the page and not the scene (the visitor's own aim), a name compared in the wrong case (the visitor's own), and a local server that refused connections under two browsers. Each was mended and the page was visited again. The page cannot be drawn: with WebGPU removed it falls back to WebGL 2, and with no canvas at all the tree and the pages still work. Both are run.

The kit's own requirements name the tests that catch their breaks Passed

The question. No requirement of the kit's own model named a test as its check, so the kill rule had no votes on that graph and L16 listed every requirement. If the names are read from the verdicts of the last pass, never written, how many requirements have a real check, how many have none, and what does L16 read?

The bar. Each requirement names the tests that actually caught breaks of its code, copied from the record. A requirement none catches is left named as such. The kill rule has votes on the rebuilt graph. L16 is reported as it reads, whether or not it falls.

How it can fail. With the catching tests removed from the verdicts no requirement may name a check; a name is never written by hand. A check named by a label with a dot in it is one test and meets the break it caught; with the old cut at the last dot it does not. L16 does not fall. The names are fitted to the record, so what it can still find is the break caught only by a crash and the requirement nothing catches. It rose from 13 listed to 12 failing and 1 listed.

A break with no verdict is drawn apart from one that got past every test Passed

The question. The fly-through painted every break without a killed-by edge red, so breaks nothing had run looked like survivors. Drawn from the verdict record, are caught, got past and no verdict three states, and does the legend name only what the graph holds?

The bar. Three states from the record on both pages, with a plant: the old rule must read more red than the new one on the same store. A legend line only for what the graph holds.

How it can fail. On the test store two breaks have no killed-by edge and one got past: the old rule paints 2 red, the page must paint 1 red and 1 violet. With the chain deleted the Reasoning line goes, and a state of a break shows only while the graph holds one. A store with no verdict table paints nothing red. On the big-store test 10 breaks have no killed-by edge, 6 got past and 4 have no verdict: red must read 6.
benchmark-tests.foot: The benchmark page

proof.head:
The proof

One command runs every proof again

98 proofs are on record. The last run, tier fast, ran 54 of them: 54 passed. The other 44 are not run in that tier, each with its reason.

Run it yourself: py -X utf8 autobot/prove_all.py --fast takes a few minutes; without --fast it runs every proof. A proof passes only if its command exits as intended, prints its checks, and where its entry states a number that number still matches the file it is read from.

Three ways a proof could pass and mean nothing

  • HANGS: the command does not finish; it is killed at its limit and reported.
  • EMPTY: the command exits cleanly having checked nothing.
  • DISAGREES: the command exits cleanly while its own lines say FAIL, or the numbers its entry states differ from the file.
proof.foot: The chain it also followsThe whole manual

proof-passed.head:
The proof

What each passing proof says

54 passed in the last run.

autobot/doc_nodes.py --selftest (C1-accuracy, C1-mechanical, C1-harm, C1-selftest)

It proves. C1-accuracy: When the loop says a manual section, slide or README paragraph describes a requirement, is that so? A wrong link is one whose document does not describe the node it is tied to. Also: C1-mechanical: For every link made by a name found in a document, does the file and line it cites really contain that name? Also: C1-harm: Adding documents to the graph must not move any other criterion, count or exit code. Did it? Also: C1-selftest: Does the tool refuse a fabricated requirement id, a renamed section, a missing file, an empty document set and an unparseable document, each in its own test?

proof-notrun.head:
The proof

What was not run, and why

44 proofs were not run in the last run. Each says why.

  • C1-held: Are the documents tool's own checks held by breaks?: A fresh pass of the tool's own code runs about 1,600 breaks and takes over an hour (the potential map's TP-self); it did not finish in 1,500 seconds beside other work.
  • PK-3: How full must the graph be before the network beats the plain rules?: Needs a graph file (the command names <graph.sqlite>) and PyTorch, and a learning curve takes minutes for each fraction and seed.
  • E1-3: Do the plan's switches hold at more seeds?: The seed script was kept in the scratch folder of the session that ran it and is not in the repository (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • GV: Can a goal be turned into a vector that points at goals worth training?: It reads a cache in the temp folder (goal_vector_cache/shops.pkl) that the experiment's earlier commands (snapshot, enumerate, measure) make first, so it fails alone in 4 minutes; it is the end of a chain, not one command.
  • T2: Can an agent finish a real task with the kit?: One agent run on a task; it is not rerun by one command (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • PK-5: Twelve agent runs, six tasks, with the loop and without it: Twelve agent runs and a blind grading (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • PK-5e: Three blind graders per pair instead of one: Six agents grade, then the tally is read; the tally tool is autobot/grade_panel.py (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • PK-5g2: Does the loop recover a lost model better, with the ids removed?: Two agent runs on one task; not rerun by one command (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T7a: A small tested class, against a public specification: Run on a licensed copy of the engine that is not in this repository (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T7b: A large, well-tested class: Run on a licensed copy of the engine that is not in this repository (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T7c: The scoring rules of a shipped open-source game: Needs a clone of the game's public repository and a restore of its packages; the requirements model is in autobot/t7/t7c/model (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T7-control: Does the loop find more defects than careful reading?: Four agent runs and three graders; not rerun by one command (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T8: Joining two finished features, does the graph name the seams?: (not shown: the words name something that is not published)
  • T3: Can the language-neutral parts model public code?: One model built by hand from a document; the builder is in the asteroids folder (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T1: Does the example run on a machine with only a newer .NET?: A one-off check on one machine (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • T4: Can a fresh agent install the kit from the zip alone?: One agent run; not rerun by one command (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • TICKS: Did each standing tick find something worth its minutes?: Each tick is an agent run (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • PASS-feature: A full pass on the game feature the loop was first built on: The loop breaks the game feature's own source in place and runs its tests, and nothing in the game project may be touched by a proof; a pass took about 23 minutes on two workers.
  • PASS-self: A pass on the loop's own code: A fresh pass of the tool's own code runs about 1,600 breaks and takes over an hour (the potential map's TP-self); it did not finish in 1,500 seconds beside other work.
  • CLOSED_LOOP_ROOT=closed_loop_kit autobot/closed_loop.py run {root}/closed_loop_kit/example/model (PASS-kit-cs): last measured at 397 s, over the 100 s that --fast allows; run without --fast
  • CLOSED_LOOP_ROOT=closed_loop_kit autobot/closed_loop.py run {root}/closed_loop_kit/example/model --chain autobot/proofs/X1_chain.yaml --no-self-improve (X1-chain): shares its model (example/model) with a run that --fast leaves out (397 s last measured), and alone it would redo that run's work
  • X4-next: The last slide says what the tool is for, and what is not measured: The build ties 22 public numbers to records in folders outside the tool copy (agi_proto/starfighter), so it refuses in a copy of the tools; its own selftest is run as the tool's selftest.
  • SELFTESTS: Does every tool have a selftest, and does it pass?: prove_all.py runs every tool's selftest itself and writes this survey (--write-survey), so this entry's command is that run and is not run twice.
  • B1: Every break of the learned parts, with a verdict: A 180-minute budget run, 245 minutes when it ran; not a proof that can be repeated in a pass.
  • SD-1: Does it matter which requirements are written first?: Needs a graph file (the command names <graph.sqlite>) and PyTorch, and a learning curve takes minutes for each choice of seed order.
  • REVIEWS: Do fresh reviewers find holes the loop passes?: Two agent runs that read the code; the reviews are autobot/research_REVIEW_1_1029.md and autobot/research_REVIEW_2_1029.md (the record says it cannot be rerun by one command)
  • X5: Does the dictation panel turn speech into text and a reply beside the slide on both pages, and keep the key in the tab?: Drives a headless browser for about 15 minutes against a built site; its own selftest, the instruments without the browser, is run as the tool's selftest.
  • X5-live: Do the real API and the real speech service let the dictation panel through, with no key at all?: Drives a headless browser against the real API and the real speech service; it is not started by a proof pass. Its own selftest is run as the tool's selftest.
  • autobot/harmony.py --prove (E1-plants): last measured at 831 s, over the 100 s that --fast allows; run without --fast
  • E2: Does every proof on record still pass when run again, together, and does the runner refuse the ways to pass without proving?: This entry's command is the run itself; running it from inside a run would start another run. Its selftest, the plants, is run as the tool's selftest.

Closed loop · prototype 0.1 · 29 October 2026

How to use AI for games

Our internal training manual at TNT Tools, adapted for Heavy Iron. The method is the closed loop: requirements first, tested by AI, so nothing is a guess.

An AI that tests the requirements before it writes the code: testing raw. The slides are the highlights. This is the whole story in plain words: what each part does, why it is there, and for every number on the slides, the test that produced it and what the number means.
